goals: Compute MAE, MSE, RMSE and R²
Choose the metric that matches the business cost
why: The metric defines what "good" means. A demand forecast judged by RMSE behaves differently from one judged by MAPE, and stakeholders care about errors in rupees or units, not abstract scores.
explain: **MAE** (mean absolute error): the average size of the miss, in the target's units. Easy to explain: "we are off by ₹3 lakh on average".
**MSE** squares each error before averaging, so big misses count far more. **RMSE** = √MSE brings it back to the original units. Use it when large errors are especially costly.
**R²**: the share of variation explained, compared with always predicting the average. 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the average, negative = worse than the average.
**MAPE** (mean absolute percentage error) is popular in forecasting ("8% off") but explodes when actual values are near zero.

formula.plain: MAE averages the absolute misses; RMSE averages the squared misses, then takes the square root.

example.title: Three predictions
example.result: RMSE > MAE because the single big miss (6) is punished more. A big gap between them signals occasional large errors.

mistakes: Reporting only R², which says nothing about error size in business units.
Using MAPE when actual values can be zero.
Comparing RMSE across datasets with different scales.
takeaways: MAE = typical miss; RMSE punishes big misses
R² is relative to the mean baseline
Pick the metric that mirrors business cost

practice.code:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
y, p = [10, 20, 30], [12, 18, 36]
print(mean_absolute_error(y, p), mean_squared_error(y, p) ** 0.5, r2_score(y, p))

check.q: Errors 1, 1, 1, 9. Which metric is most affected by the 9?

options: No better than predicting the mean
check.why: R² compares with the mean-only baseline.
